prompt: What does `@RequestMapping("/books")` on the controller class do?
hint: Look at what the paths of the two methods are once the application runs.

choices.text: It limits the whole class to GET requests
choices.why: No. It names a path and no method; `@GetMapping` and `@PostMapping` on the methods choose the method.

choices.text: It registers a servlet of its own, listening at `/books`
choices.why: There is one servlet, the `DispatcherServlet`; the annotation adds rows to its table of mappings.

choices.text: It makes the class a bean, so the component scan finds it
choices.why: That is `@RestController`, which carries `@Component` inside it. `@RequestMapping` only describes paths.

choices.text: It prefixes every method's path with `/books`
choices.why: Right. `@GetMapping("/{id}")` below it answers `/books/{id}`, and `@GetMapping` alone answers `/books`.

prompt: `GET /books/99` answered 404 with `Content-Length: 0`, and `GET /authors` answered 404 with a JSON body. Why the difference?

choices.text: Book 99 was deleted earlier, and Spring answers a request for a deleted resource with an empty 404
choices.why: Nothing was ever deleted; book 99 never existed. The difference is who wrote the answer.

choices.text: Tomcat answered `/authors` directly, before Spring saw it
choices.why: The body has Spring Boot's fields, `timestamp`, `status`, `error` and `path`. Spring did see it, and mapped it nowhere.

choices.text: The controller chose an empty 404; nothing handled `/authors`, so Spring Boot wrote that one
choices.why: Right. `ResponseEntity.notFound().build()` is a status and nothing else. A path with no mapping ends in Spring Boot's own error handling, which always writes that body.

choices.text: curl dropped the body of the first because it was sent with `-i`
choices.why: Both requests were sent with `-i`. `Content-Length: 0` is the server saying there is nothing to drop.

prompt: `DELETE /books/1` got `405` and the header `Allow: GET`. What did Spring know in order to answer that?

choices.text: That book 1 exists, and existing books cannot be deleted
choices.why: Spring never asked the service about book 1. The answer comes from the mappings alone.

choices.text: That the path matches a mapping, and only for GET
choices.why: Right. `/books/{id}` is in the table with GET and nothing else, so the method is wrong rather than the path.

choices.text: Nothing: 405 is what Tomcat answers to any DELETE
choices.why: `DELETE /authors` would be a 404, because no mapping matches that path for any method.

choices.text: That the client is not allowed to delete, which is a permission
choices.why: A missing permission is 403, and this application has no permissions until lesson 15.

prompt: The lesson sends requests with `curl -si -w '\n'`. Which statements about those flags are true? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: `-i` prints the status line and the headers before the body
choices.why: Right. Without it you see only the body, as the list of books showed.

choices.text: `-s` keeps curl from printing anything of its own, such as a progress meter
choices.why: Right. It silences curl, not the server.

choices.text: `-w '\n'` writes a newline after the answer
choices.why: Right. JSON does not end with one, and the next prompt would start on the same line.

choices.text: `-s` hides the body and keeps only the status
choices.why: The body was printed in every answer that had one. `-s` is about curl's own messages.

choices.text: `-i` turns the request into a HEAD request that asks only for headers
choices.why: That is `-I`, capital. Lower-case `-i` sends the same GET and shows more of the answer.

prompt: Put in order what happens to `GET /books/2` from the moment it reaches the application.
hint: Only one of these is your code.
items: Tomcat hands the request to the DispatcherServlet
the path text "2" becomes the long 2
the method asks the service and returns a ResponseEntity
Jackson writes the BookResponse as JSON

prompt: `GET /books/abc` was answered 400, and the method `get` never ran. At which step of the `DispatcherServlet` did the request stop?
hint: Read the exception name in the WARN line.

choices.text: Finding the method: no mapping matches `abc`
choices.why: The pattern `/books/{id}` matches any segment. The log line says the mapping was found and a conversion failed.

choices.text: Resolving the arguments
choices.why: Right. `MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException`: "abc" could not become the `long` that `@PathVariable long id` asks for.

choices.text: Inside the method, when the service found no book
choices.why: A missing book is the empty 404 of book 99. Here the method was never called.

choices.text: Writing the return value, because there was nothing to write
choices.why: There was no return value at all; the call never happened.

prompt: The bookshop grows to five controllers with twenty mapped methods between them. How many servlets does Tomcat send API requests to?

choices.text: Five, one per controller class
choices.why: A controller is a bean, not a servlet. Adding one adds rows to the mapping table.

choices.text: Twenty, one per mapped method
choices.why: The methods are rows in one table, looked up by one servlet.

choices.text: One, the DispatcherServlet
choices.why: Right. A front controller: one entrance, and the routing behind it grows with the controllers.

choices.text: None: Tomcat calls the controller methods directly
choices.why: Tomcat knows servlets and nothing about Spring's annotations; it is the dispatcher that reads them.

prompt: A tutorial writes `import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;`. What does that tell you about it, read from this course's project?

choices.text: It predates Jackson 3, whose classes moved to `tools.jackson`
choices.why: Right. That import is Jackson 2. Spring Boot 4 runs on Jackson 3, where the class is `tools.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper`.

choices.text: Nothing: that is still the package of every Jackson class
choices.why: The dependency tree showed `tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind:3.1.5`. Only the annotations kept the old package.

choices.text: It uses the annotations artifact, which is the only Jackson that Spring Boot 4 ships
choices.why: Boot 4 ships all of Jackson 3. The annotations are the part that kept `com.fasterxml`, and `ObjectMapper` is not one of them.

choices.text: It was written for Gson, the other JSON library
choices.why: Gson lives in `com.google.gson`. `com.fasterxml.jackson` is Jackson, the version before 3.

prompt: A controller returns `new Author("Machado de Assis", 1839)`, where `record Author(String name, int born)`. What JSON does Jackson write?

choices.text: `{"born":1839,"name":"Machado de Assis"}`
choices.why: The order is the record's, not the alphabet's; `name` is declared first.

choices.text: `{"getName":"Machado de Assis","getBorn":1839}`
choices.why: A record's accessors are `name()` and `born()`, and the property takes the component's name.

choices.text: `{"name":"Machado de Assis","born":1839}`
choices.why: Right: the component names, in declaration order, the `int` as a JSON number.

choices.text: `{"name":"Machado de Assis","born":"1839"}`
choices.why: An `int` becomes a JSON number, as `priceCents` did; only a `String` is quoted.

prompt: Why does the bookshop send a price as `3990` rather than `39.90`?

choices.text: JSON has no way to write a number with a decimal point in it
choices.why: JSON writes `39.9` perfectly well. The trouble starts when a program stores it as a binary fraction.

choices.text: Whole cents are exact, and 0.10 has no exact binary form
choices.why: Right. An integer count of the smallest unit is exact, and every sum of prices stays exact.

choices.text: An integer takes fewer bytes on the wire than a decimal does
choices.why: Four characters against five; nobody designs a price format around one byte.

choices.text: Jackson cannot write a `double`, only whole numbers
choices.why: It can, and would. The choice is about what a `double` does to money, not about Jackson.

prompt: In the section on POST, a client sent `"id": 1` in the body of a new book. What happened?

choices.text: Book 1 was overwritten with the new title
choices.why: Book 1 was still *Dom Casmurro* afterwards. The request record has nowhere to keep an id.

choices.text: The request was refused with 400, because `id` is not a component of `BookRequest`
choices.why: Jackson 3 ignores a property the record has no component for, with no error and no log line.

choices.text: The property was dropped and the book got the next id, 5
choices.why: Right. `BookRequest` has no `id`, so the server decided, as it should.

choices.text: The new book took id 1 and *Dom Casmurro* moved to 5
choices.why: Nothing moves an existing book. The id came from the repository's counter.

prompt: Lesson 10 turns `Book` into an entity whose author is an `Author` object. With `BookResponse` in place, what has to change so that clients still receive `"author": "Machado de Assis"`?

choices.text: Nothing: Jackson notices the change and keeps the old shape
choices.why: Jackson writes whatever it is given. Something has to turn an `Author` into the name.

choices.text: The `author` component of `BookResponse` becomes an `Author`
choices.why: Then the JSON would change shape, which is exactly what the DTO is there to prevent.

choices.text: Every client, which has to read the new nested object
choices.why: That is the cost a DTO saves: the clients never see `Author` at all.

choices.text: One line of `BookResponse.from`
choices.why: Right: the line that reads the author's name. The mapping absorbs the domain's change, and the contract stays as it was.

prompt: Match each type of the bookshop to its job.

pairs.right: what a client may send to create a book
what the API answers about a book
what the shop knows about a book

right_distractors: the JSON text exactly as it travels

prompt: What does `ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/books/" + book.id()))` add to the answer?

choices.text: Status 200 and a header with the new id
choices.why: 200 means "here it is". A creation answers 201, and the header carries a path rather than a bare id.

choices.text: A redirect, so curl fetches the new book on its own
choices.why: A 201 is not a redirect; curl printed the `Location` and asked for nothing else.

choices.text: Status 201 and the new book in the body, with nothing in the headers
choices.why: The body comes from `.body(...)`; `created(...)` is the status and the `Location` header.

choices.text: Status 201 and a `Location` header naming the new book
choices.why: Right: `HTTP/1.1 201` and `Location: /books/4` in the capture. The body is set separately, by `.body(...)`.

prompt: A POST with a perfectly good JSON body, sent with `-d` and no `-H`, was answered 415. Why?

choices.text: The JSON was malformed, and 415 is how Spring says so
choices.why: A malformed body is a 400, refused by Jackson. Here Jackson was never even asked.

choices.text: curl sends `-d` bodies as GET requests, which this path does not accept
choices.why: `-d` makes curl send a POST. A wrong method would have been a 405.

choices.text: The server could not tell which book to create, having no id in the body
choices.why: The server picks ids itself; the same body with the header created a book.

choices.text: curl labelled it as a form, and the endpoint reads only JSON
choices.why: Right. Without the header the `Content-Type` is `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, and the answer's `Accept` header lists what it does read.

prompt: Before validation existed, the body `{"isbn":"12345","title":"","author":"José de Alencar","priceCents":-5}` was stored as a book. Which checks did it pass? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: It was well-formed JSON
choices.why: Right. Jackson parsed it, or the answer would have been a 400.

choices.text: Every value fitted the type of its component
choices.why: Right. Strings into `String`s and `-5` into an `int`: types say nothing about whether a value is sensible.

choices.text: The title was checked and found acceptable
choices.why: Nothing checked the title at all; an empty string is a perfectly good `String`.

choices.text: The ISBN was checked for thirteen digits
choices.why: Nothing checked it until the custom constraint; `12345` went straight into the repository.

prompt: The constraints are on `BookRequest` and the starter is in the pom, but the parameter reads `@RequestBody BookRequest request`. What does a POST of an empty title get?

choices.text: A 201: the book is stored with its empty title
choices.why: Right, as the capture showed. Spring validates a `@RequestBody` argument only when the parameter carries `@Valid`.

choices.text: A 400, because the starter validates every record it finds
choices.why: The starter brings the validator; something still has to ask it to run.

choices.text: A compilation error, because `@NotBlank` needs `@Valid` beside it
choices.why: It compiled and ran. Unused constraints are not an error, which is what makes this mistake quiet.

choices.text: A 500, because the record breaks its own constraints when it is built
choices.why: A record does not check its annotations in its constructor; only a validator reads them.

prompt: The annotation on a controller's parameter that makes Spring check the constraints of the record Jackson built is `@___`.
Why did `priceCents` change from `int` to `Integer` when the constraints arrived?

choices.text: Bean Validation cannot read the value of a primitive component
choices.why: `@PositiveOrZero` works on an `int` as well. The difference is what happens when the price is missing.

choices.text: With `int`, a missing price silently became 0 and was stored
choices.why: Jackson 3 refused it instead, with a 400. The problem was where the refusal came from, not that it was silent.

choices.text: So that a missing price is a field error naming `priceCents`
choices.why: Right. A missing price becomes `null`, which `@NotNull` reports. With `int`, Jackson refused before the record existed, and its message named a type.

choices.text: `Integer` holds larger prices than `int` can
choices.why: Both hold the same range of values. The extra value an `Integer` can hold is `null`.

prompt: Match each request to the exception the second terminal named for it.

pairs.left: a body cut off after the ISBN
an empty title, with @Valid in place

prompt: With the final `BookRequest`, a client sends `{"isbn":"9786500000047","title":"   ","author":"José de Alencar","priceCents":null}`. How many field errors does the validator report?
hint: Check each component against each of its constraints, and remember who handles null.

prompt: The first twelve digits of an ISBN are `978650000006`. What is its check digit?
hint: Only the last digit differs from 9786500000047, and its weight is 3.

prompt: Why does `IsbnValidator.isValid` return `true` when the value is `null`?

choices.text: A null ISBN is acceptable, so a book may be created without one
choices.why: `@NotNull` beside it still refuses that book; the validator is only declining to judge.

choices.text: Null is `@NotNull`'s business, so a missing ISBN produces one error and not two
choices.why: Right, as the capture showed: one field error, `NotNull`. Every standard constraint follows the same convention.

choices.text: Calling `Isbn.isValid` with null would throw a `NullPointerException`
choices.why: `Isbn.isValid` checks for `null` itself and returns `false`. The reason is about which constraint reports.

choices.text: Bean Validation never passes `null` to a validator, so the branch is never taken
choices.why: It does pass it: that is why the convention exists and why the branch is there.

prompt: In `Isbn.isValid`, the check digit is `(10 - sum % 10) % 10`. What is the outer `% 10` for?

choices.text: So that a sum ending in 0 gives 0 instead of 10
choices.why: Right. `10 - 0` would be 10, which is not a digit, and 10 % 10 is 0.

choices.text: To keep the result positive when the sum is negative
choices.why: The sum of digits times 1 or 3 is never negative.

choices.text: To drop the 978 prefix from the calculation
choices.why: The prefix is part of the twelve digits and is weighted like the rest.

choices.text: It does nothing; it is there for symmetry with the inner one
choices.why: Try a sum of 70: without it the check digit would be 10, which is not a digit.

prompt: In the detour, `FIELD` was taken out of `@Target` on `@ValidIsbn`. What made that mistake dangerous rather than merely wrong?

choices.text: It compiled, ran and accepted the bad ISBN in silence
choices.why: Right. A constraint nobody checks looks exactly like one that passes, and only a request that should fail tells them apart.

choices.text: The build failed with an error message that is hard to read
choices.why: The build printed nothing at all. A loud failure would have been the safe outcome.

choices.text: Every request was refused, including valid ones
choices.why: The opposite: the wrong check digit was accepted with a 201.

choices.text: The log filled with warnings on every request
choices.why: There was no warning anywhere; the second terminal had nothing to say about it.

prompt: A POST to `/books` with an empty title, a JSON `Content-Type` and the final code. Put in order what happens until the client receives its 400.
hint: The method add is not in the list, because it never runs.
items: Jackson builds a BookRequest from the body
@Valid runs the validator, which finds a blank title
Spring Boot's error handling writes the 400 body

prompt: With the final code, the method `add` has just been called. What is guaranteed about the request at that moment? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Its body was JSON that Jackson could read into a `BookRequest`
choices.why: Right. Otherwise Jackson would have refused it at step 2.

choices.text: Every constraint on `BookRequest`, `@ValidIsbn` included, held
choices.why: Right. `@Valid` runs them all before the call, and any violation stops it.

choices.text: It declared a JSON content type
choices.why: Right. A form body was refused with 415 before anything else was tried.

choices.text: No book in the shop already has its ISBN
choices.why: Nothing checks that yet: a constraint sees one request, not the shop. Lesson 7 adds `DuplicateIsbnException` for it.

choices.text: The id the client sent will be the new book's id
choices.why: `BookRequest` has no id; whatever the client sent was dropped by Jackson.

prompt: A client sends a POST with a JSON `Content-Type` and the body `{"isbn":"9786500000047","title":"Iracema","author":"José de Alencar","priceCents":"free"}`. Who refuses it, and what does the log name?
hint: Two gates stand in front of the method. Which one needs a record to exist?

choices.text: The validator, with a `PositiveOrZero` field error on `priceCents`
choices.why: The validator needs a record to check, and `"free"` cannot become the `Integer` the record needs.

choices.text: Nobody: Jackson stores `null` and the book is created without a price
choices.why: Jackson refuses a value it cannot convert; it does not swap it for `null`.

choices.text: The method `add`, when the service tries to store the price
choices.why: The method never runs: both gates stand in front of it.

choices.text: Jackson, with `HttpMessageNotReadableException`
choices.why: Right, before any constraint runs. A value that cannot fit its type stops at the first gate, like the body cut off after the ISBN.
